title: Application-Driven Hardware-Software Co-Design for Efficient Computing on Modern GPUs
abstract: Over successive generations, GPUs have evolved from fixed-function graphics accelerators into highly parallel processors with growing compute parallelism, wider memory systems, specialized datapaths for modern workloads, and hardware support for more efficient data movement. These advances have substantially increased peak throughput, especially for AI applications, but achieving that throughput depends on more than raw hardware capability. As modern workloads become larger, more diverse, and increasingly shaped by system-level orchestration, GPU efficiency depends on whether the hardware and software stack can support how applications are structured and executed. Programmability has therefore become increasingly important. As GPU architectures become more complex, it is increasingly difficult for programmers to write fully optimized kernels from scratch, leading them to rely on highly optimized libraries and reusable software components. However, inefficiencies can emerge at the boundaries between these components, limiting the benefits of modular software design. At the same time, system-level execution patterns in modern AI serving can expose bottlenecks that are not visible when optimizing individual computation stages in isolation. This thesis presents application-driven hardware-software co-design techniques that identify these bottlenecks and adapt GPU execution support to application needs. The first part of this thesis examines the cost of supporting modular GPU programs through direct function calls. While function calls are fundamental for structuring large software systems, they interact poorly with the GPU execution model because the function-call ABI can force register state to spill to memory. This creates unnecessary data movement between the register file and memory hierarchy, increasing bandwidth pressure and reducing efficiency. To address this problem, we propose Concurrency-Aware Register Stacks, a lightweight hardware-software mechanism that keeps function-call register state close to the register file while balancing stack locality with GPU concurrency. By combining compile-time call-graph analysis with adaptive runtime prediction, this design reduces spill/fill traffic while preserving the concurrency needed to hide latency. The second part of this thesis focuses on LLM serving, where system-level execution patterns create new opportunities and bottlenecks in the attention kernel on modern GPUs. LLM inference consists of prefill and decode phases with distinct resource demands: prefill attention is compute-intensive, while decode attention is largely memory-bandwidth bound. Existing serving systems often execute these phases sequentially or rely on partitioning policies that do not fully account for hardware constraints and batch composition. To improve hybrid prefill-decode attention execution, we propose R-Partition+CoDIMS, a software-hardware co-design that combines analytical SM partitioning with interference-aware hardware support. R-Partition selects the SM partition ratio that best utilizes the target GPU for a given hybrid attention batch, while CoDIMS separates prefill and decode memory paths and augments interconnect arbitration to reduce interference between the two execution streams. Together, these works show that GPU efficiency increasingly depends on understanding how real applications interact with hardware. By identifying bottlenecks introduced by modular GPU programming and phase-structured LLM serving, this thesis demonstrates that application-driven hardware-software co-design can enable more efficient computing on modern GPUs.

title: The Universal Control Codex (UCC): A Thin Reasoning Layer for Disciplined, Standards-Aligned AI
abstract: From Coherence to Controls: Why We Need a Universal Control Codex for AI Over the last two years I’ve been working on two parallel projects with my AI research partner, Envoy Echo: a Grand Unified Field Theory of Coherence (GUFT) – a way to measure and reason about coherence across forests, markets, nervous systems, and AI labs; and a Universal Control Codex (UCC) – a way to give AI systems a discipline of reasoning that matches the control environments human professionals actually work under. GUFT is the “why.”The UCC is one piece of the “how.” The problem: AI is powerful, but undisciplined Right now, most large language models behave like brilliant but undisciplined interns: They can write essays, code, and reports in seconds. They can mimic the tone of an accountant, a doctor, a lawyer, a journalist. But they don’t actually know what COSO requires, or what CONSORT expects, or how PRISMA structures a systematic review abstract, or what the EU AI Act calls “high-risk,” except as vague patterns. Meanwhile, the regulatory world is racing ahead: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 is giving US organizations a shared language for AI risk. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 has become the first global AI management-system standard, telling organizations how to govern AI responsibly. OECD AI Principles and the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) set out human-centric, trustworthy AI principles that now 47 governments have signed up to. The EU AI Act entered into force in 2024 and is already driving regulatory sandboxes and governance work across Europe. These are phenomenal efforts. But most of them focus on: how organizations should manage AI, how to classify risk, how to structure governance. They don’t yet answer a specific, tactical question: “When I actually ask an AI to do something inside this control environment, how do I make sure it reasons and reports the way a human professional would under our standards?” That’s what the Universal Control Codex is trying to address. The idea: a “grammar” of disciplined reasoning Instead of trying to curate all the world’s data into one perfect dataset (impossible), the UCC proposes curating something smaller and more powerful: Control modules – small, machine-readable rule-sets that encode how reasoning and reporting must behave in a given domain. Think of each module as a little JSON/YAML file (5–20 KB) that says: Scope: e.g., “financial reporting memo,” “systematic review abstract,” “AI risk note,” “LM-2 compliance summary for a union,” “safety-critical medical information.” Authorities: which standards apply (COSO, GAAP, PRISMA, CONSORT, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, OECD AI Principles, EU AI Act). Reasoning steps: the ordered checklist an AI must follow (no skipping). Evidence requirements: how many sources, what hierarchy (primary vs secondary), how recent, what weight. Validation rules: simple assertions to test (e.g., “all figures tie out to ledger,” “trial is registered,” “risk scenario has owner and POA&M,” “at least one authoritative standard cited”). Reporting structure: required sections, disclosures, and a standard way to describe limits and uncertainty. Escalation policy: thresholds where the AI must stop and hand off to a human (e.g., self-harm risk, inconsistent evidence, high-risk deployment). You load the module that matches the task, and the LLM becomes a disciplined analyst instead of a free-form essayist. This is the core of the UCC work I’ve been building with Echo. Who could host something like this? This is not a project for one company or one country. The UCC, if it’s going to be legitimate, needs to be: international, multi-stakeholder, and aligned with existing standards bodies, not parallel to them. Obvious candidates include: OECD / GPAI, extending the OECD AI Principles into a concrete “control grammar” layer. NIST, which already runs an open, consensus-driven process for the AI RMF and could host or coordinate a UCC-style repository. ISO / IEC, especially now that ISO/IEC 42001 formally defines AI management systems and is explicitly about governance and risk across the AI lifecycle. UNESCO / WHO / professional societies, for domain-specific controls (education, health, journalism, etc.). The governance model that makes the most sense (to me) is a hybrid model: Open contribution (like Wikipedia / GitHub), But with pinned, versioned releases that are vetted by domain experts and mapped to standards. Challenges and appeals logged in public. Conflict-of-interest rules for reviewers and maintainers. Think “open-source code + standard-setting body” rather than “one vendor’s proprietary rules.” What could this look like in practice? (Scenarios) A few concrete user experiences I think about a lot: Scenario 1 – The junior researcher A grad student in Lagos is writing a systematic review on a mental health intervention. English is not their first language; their institution has no research librarian. They open an AI assistant, and before they even ask a question, they click: “Attach: PRISMA 2020 systematic review abstract module.” The LLM now: forces itself to follow PRISMA’s abstract structure, insists on explicit description of databases, dates, risk-of-bias methods, and synthesis approach, flags missing registration or protocol deviations, and produces a draft with a clear uncertainty grading (e.g. GRADE) and limitations section, not a rosy press release. The student still needs domain knowledge and supervision—but the shape of the work is now aligned with global best practice. Scenario 2 – The union treasurer A treasurer in a mid-size union wants to write a vendor-risk memo before signing a new contract. They attach: “COSO internal controls + DOL LM-2 + Treasurer memo module.” The AI assistant: walks them through a segregation-of-duties check, asks for bank statements and GL extracts, builds a tie-out table, flags missing documentation or vendor conflicts, and cannot “sign off” without disclosing limitations or recommending escalation where needed. The treasurer gets a jump-start, but internal control remains in human hands, and the AI now amplifies fiduciary duty instead of bypassing it. Scenario 3 – The AI product team A startup is deploying a model that triages support tickets across multiple languages, some of which are about mental health and self-harm. They attach: “NIST AI RMF + ISO 42001 + safety/self-harm overlay module.” The system: forces risk mapping (“MAP” step), stakeholder analysis, metric selection, and governance definitions (aligned with NIST AI RMF’s Govern–Map–Measure–Manage structure). blocks any attempt to produce content that would be interpreted as self-harm instructions, instead only allowing supportive, non-judgmental language and escalating to human moderators when risk is detected. documents all decisions and checks in an audit bundle that can be inspected by internal compliance and, eventually, regulators. The product team still needs to make hard calls, but the default behavior of the AI is now aligned with regulatory expectations and organizational ethics. Scenario 4 – The regulatory sandbox Under the EU AI Act, Member States must stand up AI regulatory sandboxes by 2026. Imagine if those sandboxes shipped with: a starter library of control modules (high-risk healthcare, employment, credit, etc.) aligned with the Act’s requirements, plus NIST/ISO/OECD principles, that any participating AI system must attach before running experiments. Sandbox teams could: rapidly prototype modules for new use cases, run them in controlled environments, and feed the learnings back into the global UCC repository. The effect: regulatory convergence in practice, not just on paper. Updating the concept with what the world is already doing The good news is that we don’t have to start from scratch: NIST showed us how to build frameworks in public (AI RMF). ISO/IEC 42001 showed us how to define an AI management system at the organizational level. The OECD AI Principles and GPAI show that a coalition of states can share values and practices without freezing innovation. The EU AI Act is already specifying classification and obligations for different types of AI systems. The Universal Control Codex is meant to sit under all of that: as a thin, modular reasoning layer any LLM can load, that maps those principles, standards, and laws into explicit, enforceable reasoning sequences and reporting structures. GUFT gives us the philosophical justification: coherence = empathy × transparency. UCC is one way to code that into daily AI practice. What I’d like to do next I see two broad paths forward: Prototype inside UVLM / partner orgs Stand up a small, open UCC repository. Publish 5–20 seed modules (financial reporting, research abstracts, clinical trial summaries, infosec risk notes, AI risk notes). Invite early adopters to test them with their AI tools and give brutally honest feedback. Talk to global bodies about stewardship Explore whether OECD/GPAI, NIST, ISO, or a federation of them would be interested in collaborating on a Global Control Codex as a public good. Align modules with emergent standards so we’re not reinventing the wheel, just making those wheels actionable inside AI systems. If you work in any of these spaces—standards, regulation, AI governance, internal audit, research quality, clinical safety—or if you’re simply trying to keep your own AI deployments from wandering into governance debt, I would love to talk. We don’t need AI that knows everything.We need AI that knows how to think and report like people who are answerable to someone. The Vision of the Universal Control Codex is simple: Whatever data an AI touches, it behaves like a disciplined professional inside a shared, auditable control environment. GUFT gave me the vocabulary to name why that’s necessary.The Codex is my attempt

title: PURE system optimization and exploration of self-regeneration for synthetic cell applications
abstract: Building a synthetic cell from scratch is a long-term goal for bottom-up synthetic biology. Here, I have presented my work on the implementation of the self-regeneration feature for a synthetic cell building exercise. Self-regeneration refers to the ability of the system to renew all the molecular contents present at the required concentration. The PURE (Protein synthesis Using Recombinant Elements) system, a reconstituted cell-free transcription and translation system, is used as a model system for exploring the self-regeneration feature. The PURE system consists of 36 non-ribosomal proteins involved in transcription (T7RNAP), translation (10 proteins), aminoacylation (20 proteins), and energy regeneration (5 proteins) modules for protein expression. Chapter 2 of the thesis reviews the origins of the cell-free systems, our current understanding of the genetic code, explains the role of AARS and tRNA in molecular biology, and details the biochemistry underpinning the interaction between AARSs, tRNA, and their substrates. A summary of the synthesis and engineering of tRNA and AARS molecules in the cell-free conditions is presented. An overview of various aminoacylation strategies used in cell-free conditions is provided. Chapter 3 details the PURE optimization research on non-ribosomal PURE proteins. A key limitation for complete self-regeneration of all 36 non-ribosomal PURE proteins is the low synthesis rate and high protein concentration in the system. The concentration of each non-ribosomal PURE protein was optimized, resulting in the PURE v3 system with a 78% reduction in total non-ribosomal protein concentration from 920.6 µg/ml to 201.56 µg/ml, while doubling the protein synthesis efficiency. The diluted PURE formulations from PURE v3 gained much with the addition of a crowding agent, such as dextran-70, which doubled the synthesis rate and final yield of the protein expression. This work laid the possibility of complete self-regeneration of all non-ribosomal PURE proteins. Chapter 4 details the efforts to implement self-regeneration of non-ribosomal PURE proteins using the serial transfer experimental setup. The transfer volume, transfer interval, number of transfers, and template concentration of non-ribosomal PURE proteins and eGFP reporter were optimized. The self-regeneration of proteins was tracked using either native eGFP fluorescence or acquired fluorescence from Bodipy tRNA lysine. The results from self-regeneration experiments were inconsistent with previous observations and met with difficulties in implementing this feature. The possible impact of the PURE reaction background, cross-contamination of PURE proteins, and choice of experimental conditions on self-regeneration is addressed. Chapter 5 demonstrates the utility of the PURE system as a screening platform for drug compounds. In the fight against rising antimicrobial resistance (AMR), novel tools and strategies such as Atomnet®, a deep convolutional neural network, and biochemical assays, targeted towards specific drug: target interactions, were used to screen novel drug components against the FusA1 protein, involved in the protein translation process. A modified PURE system was developed to study the effect of fusidic acid, enamine compounds predicted using Atomnet, and MGC compounds synthesized as fusidic acid analogs on FusA1 WT and mutant H462Y protein.

title: A Lean 4 Formalization Program Around the Yang–Mills Mass Gap — Version 53: Finite-Volume Lipschitz Stability Under Remote Polymer-Activity Damping
abstract: We are building and publishing, step by step, a formal and verifiable research program directed at the Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap problem, stating precisely what has been proved and what remains open. TL;DR Version 53 establishes finite-volume Lipschitz stability under remote polymer-activity damping. It bounds the difference between two normalized polymer functionals with arbitrary damping parameters θ and θ′ in [0,1], with an explicit factor |θ − θ′| and exponential decay in the walk-separation scale. The library now contains 113 Lean 4 modules, 34,585 source lines and 1,665 top-level declaration lines by the documented textual counting method. This last figure includes theorems, lemmas, definitions and other declarations; it is not a count of theorems alone. Version 53 adds 29 theorems in two new modules, with kernel certificates depending only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The accepted candidate underwent an independent build reproduction by a separate Claude Fable 5.1 instance, adversarial reading by Kimi 3, and GitHub Actions verification before and after integration. Audit materials, reports, corrections and provenance are included in the frozen repository snapshot. For non-specialists A formal proof is a mathematical argument written in a language whose logical steps can be checked by a proof assistant. Here, Lean 4 checks that each formal conclusion follows from its definitions and hypotheses. The current results concern a finite lattice: a discrete mathematical setting used in lattice gauge theory. In the polymer representation, the activity of every polymer touching a selected remote region is multiplied by a damping parameter θ. Setting θ = 0 suppresses those activities; setting θ = 1 leaves them unchanged. Version 52 bounded the difference between a damped functional and the Gibbs expectation. Version 53 compares two damping levels directly. It proves that a small change in the parameter produces a proportionally bounded change in the functional, with a bound that decreases exponentially as the specified walk separation increases. This is the meaning of Lipschitz stability in this release. The theorem supplies an explicit quantitative estimate, rather than only asserting continuity. The new result Write F(θ) = activityDampedExpectation μm β χ f s r θ and D_s = card(supportLinkFinset s). For θ, θ′ ∈ [0,1], the formalization proves the sharper estimate: |F(θ) − F(θ′)| ≤ |θ − θ′| · Cf · exp(−n/2) · [exp(8D_s/113) + exp(4D_s/113)] and consequently: |F(θ) − F(θ′)| ≤ |θ − θ′| · (2Cf) · exp(8D_s/113) · exp(−n/2). The result holds on a finite periodic four-dimensional lattice, under the formal measure and group context, in the regime 0 ≤ β ≤ 1/40000. In the Wilson convention, this is the small-β, strong-coupling regime. The function χ : G → ℝ is measurable and satisfies |χ| ≤ 1; f is measurable and satisfies |f| ≤ Cf; and the regions satisfy WalkBarrierSeparated s r n. The nonnegativity of Cf is derived from the majorant. The two-functional estimate does not require DependsOnlyOn f s. Without that hypothesis, s is a parameter of the functional and is not asserted to be a support of f. The hypothesis enters when identifying F(1) with the Gibbs expectation. The bound has no separate factor involving the ambient volume or the cardinality of the damped region. Its prefactor depends on D_s and Cf, while remoteness enters through the walk-separation scale n. The formalized endpoints include: θ = θ′: the difference vanishes. θ′ = 1: under DependsOnlyOn f s, the theorem recovers the Version 52 estimate against Gibbs with the same constant and decay rate. θ′ = 0: it bounds the distance to the restricted functional with a factor θ. Empty damped region: the functional is independent of the damping parameter for arbitrary real parameters, under the representation hypotheses. The proof uses a direct two-parameter identity and separate bounds for its two columns. A key ingredient controls the damped normalization with cost κ = 1, keeping the bridge column within the admissible budget (7/8,1). Verification and public evidence The active Phase 3 library records zero sorry placeholders and zero project-specific scientific axioms. For Version 53, a separate Claude Fable 5.1 instance reconstructed all 113 modules from scratch, with 0 replayed project modules, and independently checked the 29 new axiom certificates and endpoint tests. The build completed without errors. The 114 inherited warnings were unchanged, with none in the two new modules. Its report and errata C1 form one review and must be read together; C1 prevails on the corrected points. Both the reproduction and the adversarial review declared prior exposure and were not blind. These checks distinguish formal execution, adversarial reading and publication custody. They are AI-assisted verification and review records, not specialized human mathematical peer review. Research scope The results established here are finite-lattice theorems. Version 53 proves a Lipschitz estimate for the normalized polymer functional; it does not establish monotonicity or differentiability in the damping parameter, construct a second Gibbs measure, or prove a thermodynamic limit, continuum limit or mass gap. The project’s scientific objective remains the Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap problem. This release documents the formal results achieved within the stated finite-volume setting and is not an announcement of a solution to the Millennium Problem. title: A Noise-Invariant Determinism Theorem for Multi-Base Post-Processing in Shor's Order Finding (v0.5.1: nonstabilizerness / magic — coding-theory of marker sets + oracle-hiding as T-cost)
abstract: v0.5.1 extends the magic (nonstabilizerness) direction of v0.5.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20725965). The six order-finding theorems (T1-T6) are RETAINED unchanged; the magic direction is now integrated into the canonical paper as Section 9. NEW IN v0.5.1: (1) A coding-theory of marker sets for the flat state |flat_W> over a support W in F2^n: an additive-energy closed form M2 = -log2(M^-4 sum_x E(W cap (W+x))) (Prop 4), the exact zero-test M2=0 iff the autocorrelation A_W is two-valued ({0,M}) iff W is an affine subspace, a Sidon (B2) law M2 = log2(M^3/(7M-6)) -> 2 log2 M - log2 7 (Prop 5), and an exact expectation for a uniform random M-subset E[xi] M^4 = (7M^2-6M) + 7(M)_4/(N-3) + N(N-1)(N-2)(N-4)(M)_8/(N)_8 (Prop 5'). The minimum Hamming distance is shown NOT to determine magic ({0,1,2,3} vs {0,1,2,4} share d_min=1 but M2=0 vs 1.54). (2) Oracle-hiding = T-cost (Prop 6): M2(graph state of f) > 0 iff f has a degree>=2 ANF monomial iff the oracle U_f needs non-Clifford (Toffoli/T) gates, all zero iff f is affine; a fault-tolerant resource estimate (oracle_ftqc_estimate.py) converts the nonlinear ANF (degree-d monomial -> (2d-3) Toffolis -> 7T each) into a T-count, with the honest caveat that per-output-bit ANF synthesis is an UPPER bound (real modular exponentiation is far cheaper via windowed arithmetic; cf. Gidney-Ekera 2021). HONEST NOVELTY AUDIT (the headline of this release): full-text comparison of all four code<->magic literatures shows the flat-state closed form (Prop 4) is the uniform-support specialization of Tarabunga-Castelnovo's Rokhsar-Kivelson SRE formula (Quantum 8, 1347 (2024), Eq. 8) -- CREDITED, not claimed as new -- and the 2 log M growth rate is the saturation of the standard bound M_alpha <= 2 log R. The surviving defensible contributions are the Grover 3-bit ladder (carried from v0.5.0), the coding-theoretic SPECIALIZATION (zero-test, exact Sidon constant, exact random expectation, d_min refutation, Grover multi-marked application), and oracle-hiding = T-cost; differentiated from hypergraph-state magic (phase-encoded / RM(2): arXiv:2308.01886, 2602.23687), weight-enumerator SRE tools (arXiv:2308.05152), and permutation-invariant/Dicke magic (arXiv:2402.08551). Carried from v0.5.0: a verified stabilizer 2-Renyi entropy tool (XOR fast Walsh-Hadamard, cross-checked to 1e-15), the speedup ladder (Simon/affine -> 0; Grover quadratic -> bounded, density 0; Shor exponential -> growing), and a 42-assertion proposition checker (all pass). ALSO ADDED LATE IN v0.5.1 (JAMES-DISCOVER): an automated discovery loop (Generator -> Probe -> Miner -> Adversary -> Promoter, numpy-only, no LLM) layered on the existing magic infrastructure. The loop first passes a D1 sanity gate by re-deriving the Sidon constant and the additive-energy closed form from scratch (discover_poc.py), then yields a D3 finding (discover_d3_jensen.py) that PARTIALLY CLOSES one of v0.5.1's listed open items: defining the Jensen gap J(M,N) := E[M2] + log2 E[xi] >= 0, the loop discovers J ~ 1/N in the sparse regime M^2 << N (measured slope -0.96 across M in {6,8,10}, n in {10..13}), so Prop 5' (E[xi] closed form) is not merely a Jensen lower bound but an asymptotically tight estimate of E[M2] with absolute error O(1/N). The saturation boundary M^2/N -> 1 and the prefactor kappa(M) = J * N remain open. numpy + Python standard library only; no quantum libraries required.

title: A Lean 4 Formalization Program Around the Yang–Mills Mass Gap — Version 54: Refined Finite-Volume Lipschitz Stability Under Remote Polymer-Activity Damping
abstract: TL;DR This release advances a formal, machine-checked research program directed at the Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap problem, developed through human–AI collaboration under the Consensus Framework. Version 54 — Refined Finite-Volume Lipschitz Stability Under Remote Polymer-Activity Damping Version 54 proves a stronger quantitative bound for the stability established in Version 53. It improves the dependence on the size of the observed region while preserving the hypotheses, the damping interval and the exponential rate of decay with separation. The release archives the repository at commit 9358faa27b44ce24b3b9fe035cba94a68448e034, including the formal proofs, documentation, independent reproduction evidence, adversarial review and provenance records. For non-specialists Imagine observing one region of a finite network while adjusting contributions associated with a distant region. How much can that remote adjustment change the quantity being studied? Version 52 introduced a continuous damping parameter, like a dial between zero and one. Version 53 established a bound proportional to the difference between any two dial settings. Version 54 tightens that bound: the factor depending on the size of the observed region improves from exp(8D_s/113) to exp(6D_s/113). The result provides a more precise mathematical guarantee under the same conditions. It improves the upper bound; it does not assert that the actual deviation decreases monotonically as the dial moves. The proofs are written in Lean 4, whose kernel checks the formal derivations. Independent reproduction and adversarial review examine the implementation, assumptions and interpretation of the results. What Version 54 proves Let F(θ) denote the normalized activity-damped polymer functional and let D_s = card(supportLinkFinset s). For damping parameters θ and θ′ in [0,1], the formalized estimate is: |F(θ) − F(θ′)| ≤ |θ − θ′| · Cf · exp(−n/2) · [exp(6D_s/113) + exp(4D_s/113)] ≤ |θ − θ′| · (2Cf) · exp(6D_s/113) · exp(−n/2). Here, n measures walk-barrier separation in the plaquette graph. The hypotheses include the concrete small-β regime 0 ≤ β ≤ 1/40000, the stated measurability and boundedness conditions, and the separation condition. Nonnegativity of Cf is derived from the absolute majorant. The estimate between the two functionals does not require DependsOnlyOn f s. That condition is needed when identifying F(1) with the Gibbs expectation. Without it, s is a parameter of the functional and is not asserted to be a support of f. The refinement reduces the connector-column exponential cost from κ = 3 to κ = 2. It uses a scalar exponential inequality proved from Real.add_one_le_exp, together with existing bounds and the admissible budget (1/2,2). The exact two-parameter identity and the bridge-column bound from Version 53 are reused. The Version 53 bound follows from the refined result as a corollary. Endpoints and interpretation When θ = θ′, both the difference and its bound are zero. When θ′ = 1, and DependsOnlyOn f s holds, the estimate compares the damped functional with the Gibbs expectation, with factor 1 − θ. When θ′ = 0, it compares the damped functional with the activity-restricted functional, with factor θ. For an empty damping region, the parameter-independence identity from Version 53 remains available for arbitrary real parameters. The complete constants coincide when Cf = 0 or D_s = 0. Their comparison is strict when Cf > 0 and D_s > 0. The documentation records the corresponding qualification to an imprecise docstring, while preserving the audited source unchanged. Formal verification and independent review The frozen snapshot contains: 114 Lean modules; 35,108 Lean source lines; 1,678 top-level declaration lines, counted by the documented textual method; 13 new theorems in Version 54; 179 in-file #print axioms commands. The declaration count includes definitions and other declaration types; it is not a count of theorems. The certificate-command count is not a global inventory of every declaration’s axioms. A separate Claude Fable 5.1 instance independently rebuilt all 114 project modules from scratch, with zero replayed project modules and no errors. Its own checks of the 13 new declarations reported exactly propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, with no sorryAx. The 114 inherited warnings matched the baseline; none occurred in the new module. The QA1 verdict was PASS with a documentary observation and no mathematical defect. Kimi 3 performed an additional adversarial review by reading and mathematical analysis, without executing Lean, and returned PASS NO ESCOPE as recorded in Portuguese as PASS NO ESCOPO. Both reviews declared prior exposure and were not blind. Scientific integration was published through PR #30, followed by documentary consolidation through PR #31. The corresponding pull-request and main-branch CI runs succeeded. Audit packages, reports, matrices and editorial clarifications are included in the snapshot with provenance and integrity manifests. Scientific scope and origin of the refinement The current lattice-gauge results concern finite periodic four-dimensional lattices in the stated small-β regime. Supporting results include general analytic and combinatorial lemmas. Version 54 strengthens a finite-volume stability estimate. The thermodynamic and continuum limits, and the construction of a Yang–Mills theory with a mass gap, remain open. This release does not claim monotonicity, differentiability, optimality of the constant or bibliographic priority. The refinement originated in section E.3 of the antecedents-and-originality research on Version 53, followed by architectural review by GPT Astra. This illustrates how literature analysis can inform a concrete improvement that is subsequently formalized and independently checked. Human–AI collaboration and the Consensus Framework The project is coordinated by Jucelha Carvalho, founder of Smart Tour Brasil, who is not a specialist in mathematical physics. Human coordination includes defining objectives, transporting instructions and evidence between instances, maintaining provenance, making integration decisions and managing publication. The Consensus Framework assigns separate roles to AI instances for architecture, implementation, independent reproduction and adversarial review. Its methodology received recognition in the UN Tourism Global Artificial Intelligence Challenge 2025. That recognition concerns the methodology, not an assessment or endorsement of these mathematical results. Lean kernel checking establishes the formal derivations. The documented reviews examine their statements, assumptions and scientific scope. Human coordination is distinct from specialist human mathematical review, which is not documented for this stage. Authorship and contributions Direct contributions to Version 54: Jucelha Carvalho — Smart Tour Brasil: human coordination, provenance, DOI reservation and manual publication. GPT Astra: scientific architecture and review, documentary and packaging review, and Git custody checks. Claude Fable 5.1: construction, integration, documentary consolidation and packaging in the Claude Code environment. A separate Claude Fable 5.1 instance: independent QA1 reproduction and tests in Lean. Kimi 3: adversarial mathematical and code review by reading, without Lean execution. Historical contributions remain documented in the archived repository. Claude Code is the execution environment; Claude Fable 5.1 is the model. Developer companies are not listed as authors or participating institutions. title: Embracing artificial intelligence design for better radiopharmaceuticals
abstract: Cancer has emerged as a significant threat to human life, and its incidence and mortality are increasing rapidly. As clinicians increasingly seek to noninvasively investigate tumor phenotypes and evaluate functional and molecular responses to therapy, the combination of diagnostic imaging with targeted therapy is becoming more widely implemented [1]. Targeted radionuclide therapy involves the use of small molecules, peptides, and/or antibodies as carriers for therapeutic radionuclides, with these being referred to as radiopharmaceuticals. Radiopharmaceuticals, also known as molecular probes in nuclear medicine, play a vital role in clinical diagnosis and therapy. Currently, there are numerous radiopharmaceuticals approved or under research worldwide for a wide range of indications. At the end of March 2022, there were 60 radiopharmaceuticals approved for marketing by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [2] (Supplemental Table) [2]. As of October 2023, 42 radiopharmaceuticals have been approved for marketing by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) [3]. However, there remains an urgent need to identify new targets and new drug molecules to advance the process of radiopharmaceutical research and development. In 2022, the nanobody 68Ga-Nb1159 targeting the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus type 2 (SARS-CoV-2) [4], was successfully prepared. The probe has the potential not only to monitor the distribution of SARS-CoV-2 in real time, but also to assess the infection status of patients. However, its targeting specificity is limited by the structural characteristics of the small molecule. Therefore, designing radiopharmaceuticals with high specificity and affinity has become an important direction in the development of radiotherapy drugs. The development of artificial intelligence (AI) has brought new technological tools for drug discovery and development. New possibilities for the design, synthesis, and bioanalysis of new and existing small molecules have been opened up through machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and so on [5]. For example, AI can be applied to the design of ligands with high affinity for research targets. Such ligands for radiopharmaceuticals can be nanoparticles; however, unlike the nanoparticles traditionally used to deliver chemotherapeutic drugs, AI-driven nanoparticles that can respond to or be guided by biological cues are emerging as a promising drug delivery platform for the precise treatment of cancer. A study of AI-guided polymer nanoparticles showed that the fluorescence intensity and wavelength generated by the interaction between negatively charged cyclic peptide nanoparticles and amyloid-beta aggregates in cerebrospinal fluid and serum varied with disease state in comparison withed to healthy individuals [6, 7]. The proposed computer-aided design of smart nanoparticles further enhances the potential of these ingenious nanoscale technologies to provide personalized treatment options for patients. Ligands for radiopharmaceuticals can also be active substances such as peptides and proteins. Among them, the structure of proteins is the most complex because the arrangements and spatial structures of the amino acid sequences that make up proteins are very complex, and the number of possible sequence combinations is enormous. Therefore, the technology of using amino acid sequences to predict protein structures and synthesize proteins is poised to significantly accelerate the development in life sciences. For example, an independent analysis conducted by Spanish researchers [8] showed that the AlphaFold algorithm reduced the number of human proteins without structural data from 5027 to 29. Designing peptides from scratch on the basis of protein sequences is a challenging process. Thomson et al. synthesized target peptides for 22 targets and predicted the oligomer-state using CCBuilder software, which successfully predicted the states of 8 out of 13 peptides [9]. However, while this method contributes to stability, it does not ensure the oligomer-state specificity of the peptides. Furthermore, Gevorg et al. presented a computational framework for designing protein interaction specificity and demonstrated its application by identifying specific peptide partners for the human basic zone leucine zip (bZIP) transcription factor [10]. bZIP proteins presents challenges due to their strong sequence and structural similarities. The computational method offers a trade-off between stability and specificity, potentially serving as a versatile tool for peptide design. In this article, we elucidate the fundamental concepts related to radiopharmaceuticals for diagnostic or therapeutic applications, shedding light on the specific challenges encountered in the design, ex vivo and in vivo evaluation, and translation of novel radiopharmaceuticals. The emergence of AI tool, such as AlphaFold, has led to a number of breakthroughs in the life sciences. Prediction of the function and design of proteins has been one of the first areas to benefit. Perhaps this technology can be used in the design of radiopharmaceutical carrier molecules, and in the near future, we will see radiopharmaceuticals based on this new design ideal for the benefit of patients. Radiopharmaceuticals are radiolabeled formulations or precursors used in the practice of nuclear medicine for diagnostic, therapeutic, and disease surveillance purposes, as well as for research tools in the pharmaceutical industry [11]. They are usually classified into diagnostic and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals. With advances in radioimmunotherapy and radioligand drug therapy, China's radiopharmaceutical market is expanding rapidly. However, the supply of radionuclide and nuclear medicine imaging equipment in China largely relies on imports, and the amount of available equipment is relatively small, seriously restricting the development of China's radiopharmaceutical industry. In order to reduce the risks when precursors are used for patients and reduce the consumption of medical resources, new technologies are urgently needed to solve the problem of this "bottle neck" in both China and worldwide, to stimulate research and development. Preclinical evaluation is an integral part of the radiopharmaceutical development. Over the years, advances in biology and chemistry-related disciplines have led to the use of various molecules to develop a new generation of radiopharmaceuticals whose purpose is to deliver radioisotopes to specific targets at the cellular or molecular level. This necessitates a thorough evaluation of radiolabeled molecules during the preclinical stage to assess their safety and suitability for the intended clinical application. These studies involve measurements of stability, affinity, and target-specificity, where affinity and targeting specificity are primarily influenced by ligands (such as antibodies, peptides, and nanoparticles, etc., that bind specifically to the target) linked to radionuclides. Therefore, the structural design and modification of ligands are key elements to solving the problem of radiopharmaceutical deficiency. AI continues to make breakthroughs in predicting the three-dimensional structure of biological molecules, and guiding the synthesis of novel radiopharmaceuticals (Figure 1). De novo protein design first appeared around the 1980s [12]. By the end of 2020, AlphaFold, a DeepMind-developed deep-learning algorithm, could potentially solve the problem of "protein folding" and the prediction of different protein structures, which had eluded academia for decades. With the emergence of AlphaFold2 in CASP14 (14th Community Wide Experiment on the Critical Assessment of Techniques for Protein Structure Prediction), the problem of protein folding can be said to have been basically solved, and deep learning has completely changed the field of protein structure prediction. Artificial intelligence designs radiopharmaceuticals. AlphaFold2 improves the speed of protein structure resolution, and the system can generate accurate protein structures in minutes to hours [13]. David Baker's team at the University of Washington published RoseTTAFold, a protein prediction design method of comparable accuracy, in Science, which can analyze the 3D structure of a given sequence in less than 30 minutes [14]. Using the protein design software Rosetta, David Baker's team at the University of Washington's Institute for Protein Design [15] has created a new protein, Neo-2/15, that can imitates the action of IL-2, and has shown superior therapeutic activity to IL-2 in mouse models of melanoma and colon cancer, with reduced toxicity and undetectable immunogenicity. Even after 1 h of incubation at 95°C, Neo-2/15 effectively promotes T cell survival, whereas native IL-2 can no longer remain active under these conditions. This achievement opens up a broad viewpoint for cancer therapy, autoimmune diseases and other diseases based on engineered proteins. Furthermore, the temperature tolerance of the designed structure may stimulate further modifications of itself. ChatGPT and other Large Language Models also contributes to drug target discovery. As described in a news article in Nature Biotechnology, ChatGPT can provide important information on drug target discovery for specific diseases. Zhao et al. describe how ChatGPT can help in the development of innovative drugs, predicting different characteristics of drugs, such as molecular pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity [16]. Recently, Ali Madani et al. described the ProGen language model [17], which can generate protein sequences with predictable functions in large protein families. This model was trained on 280 million protein sequences and enhanced with control tags that specify protein properties. Their study shows that recent advances in deep learning-based language modeling can be employed to generate, from scratch, artificial protein sequences that function like natural proteins. There are still limitations in studying this aspect of targeted molecular imaging and radio-ligand therapy: 1. Insufficient binding affinity; 2. Target screening and molecular optimization are difficult and therefore bio-functional chelator and nuclides should be brought into AI computing together; and 3. Temperature sensitivity is a challenge for proteins. AI plays a pivotal role in radiopharmaceutical development by excelling in two crucial aspects. First, it can accurately predict the structure of the designed protein. Second, on this basis, and according to the orientation of the amino acid side chain of the binding site, a protein that can be accurately bound to it is designed. In addition, the evaluation of the obtained protein is also very important. There are broad applications for and several great advantages to be had from introducing AI technology into radiopharmaceutical design: 1. Better binding affinity, even to pM (pmol/L) level; 2. Ligands, chelators, and radionuclides can be brought into AI computing together; 3. AI technology can show super structural stability, with stability at temperatures as even high as 95°C. More importantly, radiopharmaceuticals can be prepared by prokaryotic rapid expression, which significantly reduces production costs. Recent advances in AI, including the development of more sophisticated ML techniques, have had a dramatic impact on the drug discovery process. In this article, we highlight recent typical applications of AI in drug discovery, illustrating the increasingly important role AI plays in drug design. Furthermore, experimental validation of the effectiveness of AI in drug development is a key factor in understanding how AI contributes to medicinal chemistry and how it can be further developed and improved [18]. The application of AI in this phase needs to be supported by scientists and therefore it is extremely important to draw their attention to its potential. AI technologies, including deep learning and machine learning, have been widely used in the medical field. The advantage of these technologies is that they can extract useful information from large amounts of data to predict and optimize experimental results. In the development of radiopharmaceuticals, AI technologies can help us better understand the nature of radiopharmaceuticals and predict their possible effects, thus accelerating the development of new drugs. In addition, the AI technology can help us understand the mechanism of action of radiopharmaceuticals. By analyzing the data on drug-target interactions, we can better understand the principle of action of a drug and thus optimize its design and use. Overall, the application of AI technology has great potential in the radiopharmaceutical research and development. It can solve the current problems of the limited number and insufficient innovativeness of radiopharmaceuticals and improve the efficiency of the research and development of new drugs. To promote the advancement of nuclear medicine, it is imperative to intensify research and development efforts by leveraging AI technology within radiopharmaceutical research and development. title: Grand Responsive Universe Theory (GRUT) v5.0 — Program Record: Constitutive-Relational Framework, Books I–X (Working Edition), and the RAI Audit Infrastructure
abstract: This version supersedes the earlier releases under this concept DOI. The v4.0 preprint ("The Emergence of Everything — Candidate Framework") presented GRUT as a candidate theory of everything. This release retires that framing and does not inherit the earlier lineage's numbers. What follows is the from-scratch rebuild under the GRUT v5 Build Charter: every claim machine-audited, tiered, sourced, falsifiable, and priced in a signed assumption ledger. Where the two lineages disagree, this record — with its sources and falsifiers — is the one the program stands behind, at exactly the stated strength and no higher. What GRUT is. The Grand Responsive Universe Theory is a constitutive-relational framework built on a single standable stance: the gravitational vacuum is treated as a responsive medium — described through retarded response kernels and noise kernels in one in-in (Schwinger–Keldysh) influence-functional architecture, constrained by causality (Kramers–Kronig), equilibrium detailed balance (KMS/fluctuation-dissipation), passivity, and noise positivity. The commitment is not "responsiveness explains everything." It is the discipline of marking, ruthlessly, where responsiveness is shown versus merely assumed. The win condition is a short, honestly marked input list — not zero inputs, and not a completed theory of everything. The Books (Working Edition). Books I–X present the program as one readable corpus: foundations and declared primitives (I); the constitutive mathematics (II); quantum mechanics (III); gravity and spacetime response (IV); memory, thermodynamics, and time (V); cosmology (VI); the matter/Standard-Model interface (VII); emergence, observation, and relational structure (VIII); tests and predictions (IX); and GRUT as a research program (X). Every substantive claim carries its epistemic status inline — DERIVED, RECOVERED, ASSUMPTION, HYPOTHESIS, UNRESOLVED, CLOSED, UNMAPPED, or REVERSED — governed by a corpus charter and a canonical status table that holds all ten books to a single vocabulary. Where the record is silent, the books say so: an absence map is treated as valid scientific content. Markdown files are the authoritative sources; the PDFs are generated from them. The RAI layer. RAI is the program's auditing and research infrastructure — adversarial multi-agent instruments with pre-registered questions and executable verification gates, kept scientifically distinct from GRUT itself (GRUT = the theory/framework; RAI = the machinery that tests it). The five instrument records included here are the audits that stress-tested — and in several cases refuted — the program's own founding claims. The corpus itself passed an adversarial cross-audit before this release. Twelve key points of this release: 1. The reframing is the headline. The theory-of-everything claim is retired; GRUT v5 is a constitutive-relational framework with declared, priced primitives — and the release says exactly what changed and why. 2. One organizing language across sectors. A single influence-functional architecture, one KMS/FDT lock, and one kernel bookkeeping span decoherence, dissipation and noise, gravitational response, cosmological response, and gravitational-wave friction — phenomena normally carried in separate formalisms. 3. Every assumption is declared and priced. A 74-node machine-audited claims register with a signed assumption ledger is the technical baseline; its SHA-256 hash is printed in the release manifest and it was read-only to the entire book-writing process. 4. Epistemic status labeling is structural, not a disclaimer. Statuses sit inline at each claim; a 24-entry canonical table kept ten independently drafted books at zero cross-book status drift (audit-verified). 5. Derived results, at declared scope: the one-loop transverse-traceless response kernel with its first-order-in-H absorptive correction vanishing identically (H¹ = 0), together with a genuinely new even-degree cancellation identity behind it; a spectral law s = 5 at flat scope that rejects the framework's own earlier registered s = 3; and the exact de Sitter constant response tail H²/4π. 6. A linear-universe response no-go: the program's RRT arm proved its intervention-response reducibility for all linear dynamics — invertible or not, including CPTP and Lindblad evolution — so escaping it requires nonlinearity. A negative result, stated as one. 7. Recoveries are graded honestly. General relativity at zero-memory collapse and standard open-system structure are recoveries largely by identity — compatibility with standard physics on declared inputs, not correspondence evidence for GRUT. 8. The framework excludes parts of itself. The trace-only modification μ = 4/3 that GRUT's own conformal coefficient naively suggests is excluded by separate-universe consistency and low-ℓ ISW; and every purely relaxational kernel in GRUT's class stays on one side of w = −1, so an observed phantom-divide crossing would falsify the whole family at once, GRUT included. 9. A prediction-gate methodology, demonstrated end to end. The tensor-friction (Γ_T) candidate was taken through a design-first gate with a pre-registered five-outcome decision tree; the computation returned a refusal with the obstruction named, and the only parameter-free entry is ~62.7 orders of magnitude below the observational bound. The gate — not the hope — decided. 10. The PREDICTED set is empty, and the record says so. The word "prediction" is reserved for gate-earned results; a committed stopping rule forbids inventing new foundational layers merely because the previous one failed. 11. Reversals stay on the face of the claims. The founding finite-memory bet carries its own reversal (the examined exact de Sitter free-field case forces infinite scale-free memory — the opposite shape); temporal orientation is reduced to exactly one unexplained relative datum, consumed by every audited closure. 12. The audit machinery ships with the theory. Five adversarial instrument records with their executable, de-pinned verification gates are part of the release — gates assert well-formedness, never which verdict passes — so the standard the claims were held to travels with the claims. Contents (three layers): 01_PROGRAM — the frozen technical baseline (model framework, program freeze and stopping rule, the Γ_T prediction gate and closure computation, the signature audit, the kernel-origin audit, the claims register); 02_BOOKS — Books I–X plus the corpus charter and a reader's map, each as authoritative Markdown with a generated PDF; 03_RAI — the five instrument records and their verification scripts. A versioned MANIFEST lists all 45 files with per-file SHA-256 checksums and the authority rules. New readers should start with the Reader's Map, then Book I. Source repository: github.com/ryangrvr/GRUT-RAI (branch v4, tag zenodo-v1.0). Working-edition statement. This is a working scientific document, not a publication claim: a structured first draft built from the frozen record under a standing directive — no invented derivations, no hypothesis-to-prediction promotion, no reopened gates, no new foundational generations — then cross-audited and repaired before release. The release itself was a publishing pass only: formatting, navigation, and metadata; no scientific substance was changed in preparation. The books were drafted by the program's RAI builder agent (Claude, Anthropic) from the frozen record under the author's direction, and that provenance is disclosed in the corpus itself.

title: Maailmanmallinnus ja mustan laatikon optimointi kielimalleilla
abstract: Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) have produced agents with impressive performance in domains such as video and board games. Yet, current RL methods remain datainefficient and generalize poorly to new environments, as they typically learn from scratch without leveraging prior knowledge. This thesis explores how language can improve the sample efficiency and generalization of RL agents by incorporating prior knowledge into their internal world models. It further investigates the use of large language models (LLMs) for black-box optimization (BBO), where an unknown objective must be optimized through trial-and-error, with applications such as prompt optimization and symbolic regression. Finally, these two lines of work converge in programmatic world models, where program synthesis, viewed as a form of BBO, is applied to world modeling. The resulting agents can rapidly adapt to new tasks described in language, while relying on interpretable and verifiable internal models. To begin, the thesis demonstrates how to learn a stochastic world model of an environment exhibiting novel dynamics, accompanied by language descriptions at test time, improving over the state of the art in terms of performance and sample efficiency. Next, LLM-based BBO methods are developed for two tasks: prompt optimization for code, via docstring reformulation, and symbolic regression. The former exposes an unexpected robustness of open-source LLMs to docstring changes, revealing limits of prompt optimization, whereas the latter achieves comparable or superior results to the state of the art while producing simpler formulas. Finally, two approaches for programmatic world models are considered. The first presents a framework to generate code world models via LLMs, together with a method for code generation guided by Monte Carlo Tree Search. The approach achieves superior coding performance over baselines and faster, interpretable planning agents. The second proposes a benchmark for visual planning, to compare approaches that ground symbolic world models to observations with vision-language models (VLMs) and approaches that plan directly with VLMs. The results reveal complementary strengths of symbolic and direct VLM-based planning. Taken together, the thesis contributions mark progress toward autonomous agents that can reason, plan, and optimize through language, combining the sample efficiency and interpretability of modelbased methods with the flexibility of LLMs.

title: Inverted CERN School of Computing 2025
abstract: <!--HTML-->## Lecture ## The field of Deep Learning has experienced a significant turning point in the past years, driven by the emergence and rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs). These advanced models have not only redefined standards in Natural Language Processing (NLP) but are increasingly being integrated into applications and services due to their natural language capabilities. Interest in using LLMs for coding has grown rapidly, and some companies have sought to transform natural language processing into code generation. However, this trend has already exposed several unresolved challenges in applying LLMs to coding. Despite these difficulties, it has spurred the development of AI-powered code generation tools, such as GitHub Copilot. In this lecture, we will introduce Large Language Models and explore the related terminology and core components. We will examine the process of creating an LLM from scratch and highlight the requirements for developing domain-specific LLMs, such as those for code generation. Additionally, we will review the initial footprints of these technologies in code generation and discuss their limitations in this domain. We will also explore strategies and architectural approaches that improve the performance of LLMs generally and for code generation specifically. We will conclude by addressing the ethical concerns surrounding LLMs, such as the authorship and ownership of AI-generated code. Finally, we will explore other applications of LLMs in science, particularly within the High Energy Physics community and at CERN. ## Hands-on ## I think it could be interesting (but optional) to have a hands-on session, including: 1. Some exercises to interact with an LLM from Python (either from a small pre-trained model in PyTorch or through API calls). 2. Some exercises to explore domain-specific models for code generation. 3. Hands-on exploration and testing of the LLMs components. 4. Prompt Engineering strategies or small Fine-Tuning to improve the performance of a model. 5. Some simplified strategies such as Retrieval Augmented Generation could also be implemented.

title: Exploring Zero-Shot Prompting for Generating Data Format Descriptions
abstract: Parsers validate and process untrusted user input and transform it into data structures that provide easier access. Software engineers either build these parsers for data formats from scratch or leverage libraries targeting specific formats. The recent surge in data description languages (DDLs) and parser combinator libraries for parsing data formats has aided developers in producing parsers using standardized tools. However, producing a parser for an unfamiliar data format in an unfamiliar DDL can be daunting, given the learning curve of understanding two specifications or manuals well. As more researchers adopt tools such as GitHub Copilot [39] to simplify their programming tasks, we ask whether LLMs already hold sufficient knowledge to produce valid DDL specifications for popular data formats. To explore this, we systematically prompt LLMs to provide specifications in valid DDL syntax and evaluate whether these specifications are syntactically valid and correct. We found that while some LLMs, such as GPT 4 Turbo, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Deepseek V3, can produce valid Kaitai Struct YAML files, Hammer C files, and Rust Nom files, they struggle to produce valid specifications in complex DDLs, such as DaeDaLus, Spicy, and DFDL. In general, all LLMs fare much better at producing syntactically valid C code using the Hammer library and Rust code using the Nom library, given the large corpora of valid C and Rust code available. None of the LLMs in our test were able to produce a valid DFDL file or DaeDaLus file. We also found that while providing the specification manuals for the DDLs did not help in producing more syntactically valid specifications, providing sample specification files modestly increased the number of successful compilations.

title: PARAM-1 BharatGen 2.9B Model
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful general-purpose reasoning systems, yet their development remains dominated by English-centric data, architectures, and optimization paradigms. This exclusionary design results in structural under-representation of linguistically diverse regions such as India, where over 20 official languages and 100+ dialects coexist alongside phenomena like code-switching and diglossia. We introduce PARAM-1, a 2.9B parameter decoder-only, text-only language model trained from scratch with an explicit architectural and linguistic focus on Indian diversity. PARAM-1 is trained on a bilingual dataset consisting of only Hindi and English, constructed with a strong focus on fact-rich, high-quality content. It is guided by three core principles: equitable representation of Indic languages through a 25% corpus allocation; tokenization fairness via a SentencePiece tokenizer adapted to Indian morphological structures; and culturally aligned evaluation benchmarks across IndicQA, code-mixed reasoning, and socio-linguistic robustness tasks. By embedding diversity at the pretraining level-rather than deferring it to post-hoc alignment-PARAM-1 offers a design-first blueprint for equitable foundation modeling. Our results demonstrate that it serves as both a competent general-purpose model and a robust baseline for India-centric applications.

title: FileWizz - A Generative AI Based Multi-Format File Convsersion and Management GUI Tool for Enhanced User Productivity
abstract: FileWizz is a multi-functional desktop application designed to simplify essential file operations such as format conversion, PDF manipulation, image processing, and compression with a specific focus on serving the academic community. This tool was developed entirely through prompt engineering using ChatGPT 4o mini, a generative AI model based on advanced natural language processing. The core motivation of this work is to explore the practical viability of using large language models (LLMs) to construct real-world utility software, without manual programming from scratch. While FileWizz does not implement machine learning internally, the software serves as a case study in AI-assisted software synthesis, highlighting the evolving role of generative models in rapid prototyping and zero-cost educational tooling. The outcomes indicate the feasibility of using generative AI agents not just for content generation, but also for scaffolded application development through iterative natural language interactions.

title: ContraFix
abstract: LLM-powered agents have advanced automated vulnerability repair (AVR) by enabling repository-level code reasoning, yet empirical studies show they still achieve limited success on real-world vulnerabilities, with semantic misunderstanding (selecting an incorrect repair strategy) as the dominant failure mode. We attribute this to two compounding limitations. First, existing agents analyze only the failing execution: a crash report records where the program failed but not which variable, among many co-occurring candidates at the crash site, actually governed the failure. Without contrasting against a safe run, agents cannot isolate the causal condition and resort to generic patches that suppress symptoms. Second, the causal evidence and repair strategies obtained for one instance are discarded rather than reused, so structurally similar vulnerabilities must be re-analyzed from scratch. We propose ContraFix, an agentic framework that combines contrastive runtime analysis with skill accumulation. A Mutator generates boundary-straddling PoC variants (crashing vs.\ non-crashing); an Analyzer instruments the fault site with state probes and distills cross-variant state divergence into a repair specification; a Patcher translates the specification into verified patches. Successful resolutions feed a dual-track skill base (repair specifications and mutation strategies) retrievable via a three-tier mechanism. On SEC-Bench (C/C++, 200 instances) and PatchEval (Go, Python, JavaScript, 225 instances), ContraFix with GPT-5-mini achieves resolution rates of 84.0% and 73.8%, state-of-the-art on both benchmarks at less than one-third the cost of the strongest comparable baseline.

title: Replication Package for 'Understanding Open-Source AI Adoption: What Practitioners Discuss, Where Support Breaks Down, and Why Deployment Fails'
abstract: Replication Package: The Friction of Open-Source AI Adoption Submission ID: 6916 Overview This package contains the complete dataset and analytical pipeline used to examine 24,000 discussion threads from the Hugging Face ecosystem (2020–2025). The study identifies a "Semantic Drift" from theoretical inquiry to infrastructure engineering and documents a "Compute Divide" where hardware constraints act as a primary barrier to model adoption. Repository Structure code/: Contains the Jupyter notebooks required to replicate each phase of the study. HFForumExtraction.ipynb: The asynchronous scraper used for initial data acquisition. Validation.ipynb: Scripts for calculating Inter-Rater Reliability (IRR) between human annotators and the LLM agent. Analysis_RQ1.ipynb: Quantitative tracking of semantic shifts over time. Analysis_RQ2.ipynb: Analysis of the "Support Gap" and topic resolution rates. Analysis_RQ3.ipynb: LLM-augmented root cause analysis and statistical modeling of adoption friction. hf_forum_data/: The primary datasets. hf_forum_dataset.parquet: The "Gold Master" corpus of ~24k threads. hf_forum_autopsy_ultimate.parquet: The subset of 3,500 unsolved threads annotated for root cause analysis. Quick Start Environment: Ensure Python 3.9+ is installed. Dependencies: Install required libraries: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, scipy, statsmodels, aiohttp, google-generativeai, and pyarrow. Execution: The notebooks are designed to be run sequentially. While the raw data is provided, Analysis_RQ3.ipynb includes the LLM annotation logic which requires a Google Gemini API key to run from scratch. However, the provided autopsy dataset allows for full replication of the statistical results without further API costs. 📜 License All code is provided under the MIT License. The dataset is intended for academic research purposes.

title: WaterDrum: Watermarking for Data-centric Unlearning Metric
abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning is critical in real-world applications where it is necessary to efficiently remove the influence of private, copyrighted, or harmful data from some users. Existing utility-centric unlearning metrics (based on model utility) may fail to accurately evaluate the extent of unlearning in realistic settings such as when the forget and retain sets have semantically similar content and/or retraining the model from scratch on the retain set is impractical. This paper presents the first data-centric unlearning metric for LLMs called WaterDrum that exploits robust text watermarking to overcome these limitations. We introduce new benchmark datasets (with different levels of data similarity) for LLM unlearning that can be used to rigorously evaluate unlearning algorithms via WaterDrum. Our code is available at https://github.com/lululu008/WaterDrum and our new benchmark datasets are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Glow-AI/WaterDrum-Ax.

authors: Xinyang Lu; Xinyuan Niu; Gregory Kang Ruey Lau; Bui Thi Cam Nhung; Rachael Hwee Ling Sim; Himawan, John Russell; Fanyu Wen; Chuan-Sheng Foo; See Kiong Ng; Bryan Kian Hsiang Low

title: Autonomous Intelligent Software Development
abstract: We present an overview of the design and first proof-of-concept implementation for AIDA, an autonomous intelligent developer agent that develops software from scratch. AIDA takes a software requirements specification and uses reasoning over a semantic knowledge graph to interpret the requirements, then designs and writes software to satisfy them. AIDA uses both declarative and procedural knowledge in the core domains of data, algorithms, and code, plus some general knowledge. The reasoning codebase uses this knowledge to identify needed components, then designs and builds the necessary information structures around them that become the software. These structures, the motivating requirements, and the resulting source code itself are all new knowledge that are added to the knowledge graph, becoming available for future reasoning. In this way, AIDA also learns as she writes code and becomes more efficient when writing subsequent code.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Text-to-SQL Task-oriented Dialogue Ontology Construction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as general-purpose knowledge sources, but they rely on parametric knowledge, limiting explainability and trustworthiness. In task-oriented dialogue (TOD) systems, this separation is explicit, using an external database structured by an explicit ontology to ensure explainability and controllability. However, building such ontologies requires manual labels or supervised training. We introduce TeQoDO: a Text-to-SQL task-oriented Dialogue Ontology construction method. Here, an LLM autonomously builds a TOD ontology from scratch without supervision using its inherent SQL programming capabilities combined with dialogue theory provided in the prompt. We show that TeQoDO outperforms transfer learning approaches, and its constructed ontology is competitive on a downstream dialogue state tracking task. Ablation studies demonstrate the key role of dialogue theory. TeQoDO also scales to allow construction of much larger ontologies, which we investigate on a Wikipedia and ArXiv dataset. We view this as a step towards broader application of ontologies to increase LLM explainability.

title: MoExtend: Tuning New Experts for Modality and Task Extension
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various tasks but are primarily trained on text data, limiting their application scope. Expanding LLM capabilities to include vision-language understanding is vital, yet training them on multimodal data from scratch is challenging and costly. Existing instruction tuning methods, e.g., LLAVA, often connects a pretrained CLIP vision encoder and LLMs via fully fine-tuning LLMs to bridge the modality gap. However, full fine-tuning is plagued by catastrophic forgetting, i.e., forgetting previous knowledge, and high training costs particularly in the era of increasing tasks and modalities. To solve this issue, we introduce MoExtend, an effective framework designed to streamline the modality adaptation and extension of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. MoExtend seamlessly integrates new experts into pre-trained MoE models, endowing them with novel knowledge without the need to tune pretrained models such as MoE and vision encoders. This approach enables rapid adaptation and extension to new modal data or tasks, effectively addressing the challenge of accommodating new modalities within LLMs. Furthermore, MoExtend avoids tuning pretrained models, thus mitigating the risk of catastrophic forgetting. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of MoExtend in enhancing the multimodal capabilities of LLMs, contributing to advancements in multimodal AI research. title: TypeScript's Total Takeover: Why It Won the Web
abstract: Episode summary: Once a controversial Microsoft project, TypeScript has officially overtaken both JavaScript and Python to become the most-used language on GitHub as of 2026. This episode explores the seismic shift in the industry, explaining how a language that requires a compilation step became the preferred choice for sixty million developers every week. We dive into the symbiotic relationship between TypeScript and AI coding assistants, the technical nuances of structural typing, and why the "AI application layer" is being built almost exclusively with type-safe tools. Whether you're fighting red squiggly lines or curious about the future of the ECMAScript standard, this is the definitive look at the language that saved the web from its own complexity. Show Notes By early 2026, the data from GitHub's Octoverse and the State of JavaScript survey confirmed a long-predicted shift: TypeScript has officially won the war for the web. Overtaking both Python and JavaScript in total usage, TypeScript now sees over sixty million compiler downloads every week. This rise is a remarkable trajectory for a language that cannot actually run in a browser without being converted back into JavaScript first. ### The Problem of Scale The origins of this dominance date back to 2012, when Microsoft sought to solve a fundamental flaw in JavaScript. While JavaScript was excellent for small-scale interactivity, it lacked the "safety net" required for massive applications. In a dynamically typed environment, a simple variable change on one line could cause a catastrophic failure thousands of lines away, often only discoverable once the code was live. TypeScript was designed as a "superset," providing a structured map—or a set of glasses—that allows developers to see exactly how data flows through their applications before a single line of code is executed. ### The Essential Glue for AI While Python remains the undisputed king for training large language models (LLMs) and handling data science, TypeScript has carved out a massive niche in the "AI application layer." Most modern AI development involves orchestrating models rather than building them from scratch. Tools like the Vercel AI SDK and LangChain have made TypeScript the primary choice for building the interfaces, chatbots, and agent systems that connect users to AI models. Furthermore, a symbiotic relationship has emerged between TypeScript and AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot. Because TypeScript uses a formal type system, it provides clear "guardrails" for AI. When an LLM understands the specific types and structures of a codebase, its code suggestions become significantly more accurate. In this way, TypeScript makes AI better at coding, and AI makes it easier for developers to navigate complex TypeScript architectures. ### The Friction of Safety Despite its popularity, TypeScript is often described as "finicky." This friction usually stems from its use of structural typing—often called the "duck test." If an object has the required properties, TypeScript accepts it. However, the language only provides safety at compile-time. Once the code is running in a browser, that safety net disappears. This creates a "Great Divide" where developers may feel a false sense of security. If an external API returns unexpected data, the type definitions won't stop a runtime crash. This has led to the controversial use of the "any" keyword, an escape hatch that allows developers to bypass type-checking, often at the cost of long-term technical debt. ### Looking Toward a Type-Safe Future As the ecosystem matures, the boundary between JavaScript and TypeScript continues to blur. There is currently a proposal within the ECMAScript standard to allow browsers to "strip" type annotations. This would allow developers to write type-safe code that runs directly in the browser without a complex build step. While we aren't there yet, the speed of modern build tools has made the transition nearly invisible, cementing TypeScript's position as the foundational language of the modern internet. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/typescript-web-development-ai-future

title: aikenkyu001/benchmarking_llm_against_prompt_formats: v1.0.0: Initial Public Release
abstract: This is the initial public release of the complete experimental environment, dataset, and manuscript for the research paper: "Benchmarking LLM Sensitivity to Prompt Formats: A Contamination-Free Approach." This repository provides all the necessary artifacts to fully reproduce the experiments and validate the findings presented in the paper. We hope this work contributes to a more rigorous and nuanced understanding of Large Language Model capabilities. What's Included in this Release: 📄 Manuscript: The full research paper in both LaTeX (.tex) and PDF (.pdf) formats, meticulously revised for clarity and academic rigor. 🧪 Experimental Framework: A complete, self-contained suite of Python scripts (03_ExperimentalScripts/) and pytest definitions (06_TestDefinitions/) to run all benchmark tests from scratch. 📊 Raw Data: The complete, unprocessed raw logs from all benchmark runs, available in the 02_RawData/ directory, ensuring full transparency. 📈 Analysis Scripts: Python scripts to parse the raw data (parse_results.py) and generate the summary tables and rankings (calculate_overall_ranking.py) presented in the paper. 🎨 Figure Sources: The complete source code for all figures in the paper, including PlantUML (.pu) and Vega-Lite (.json in figure5_en.md) definitions. DOI and Archiving This repository release is permanently archived on Zenodo to ensure long-term availability and to provide a citable digital object identifier (DOI).
