title: Correction: Thinking out of the (Olympic) box: is it time to reconsider permanent hosting for sustainable Olympics? A conceptual review
abstract: The modern Olympic Games embody a profound paradox. Conceived by Baron Pierre de Coubertin as a vehicle for international understanding, peace, and athletic excellence, the Games have evolved into what economists describe as a "moneylosing proposition" [(1), p. 201], what environmental scientists characterize as exhibiting "declining sustainability performance" [(2), p. 340], and what political scientists identify as "repeatedly lead[ing] to political disruptions and boycotts" [(3), p. 148]. The institution created to unite humanity has become inextricably linked with division, sovereign debt, and environmental degradation, threatening its long-term viability. This persistence of challenges across diverse contexts-different nations, political systems, economic conditions, and decades-suggests that the problems stem from structural features of the Olympic model itself rather than from inadequate oversight, raising fundamental questions about whether incremental reforms can ever be sufficient.Empirical evidence reveals patterns suggesting these are not isolated failures but systemic pathologies embedded in the rotational hosting model. Every Olympic Games from 1968 to 2012 exceeded its original budget, with average cost overruns exceeding 150 percent-ranging from 156% to 179% depending on the dataset and time period analyzed (1,4). Recent Games have reached absolute costs that challenge the economic rationality of hosting: Beijing 2008 spent $40 billion, Sochi 2014 reached $55 billion, and Tokyo 2020 reached $15.4 billion-with some estimates approaching $20 billion-despite pandemic-related reductions in spectator services (1,(5)(6)(7). The 16 Summer and Winter Games between 1992 and 2020 collectively cost tens of billions of dollars, yet sustainability assessments found declining performance over time rather than improvement (2). Khraiche and Alakshendra (8) document that "in the last 50 years, every Olympics has experienced a major cost overrun" (p. 845), establishing this as a systemic pattern rather than an occasional failure attributable to poor planning in specific host cities.The pattern is remarkably consistent. It spans both pluralistic and centralized governance models, as well as wealthy and developing nations. This consistency demands an explanation beyond individual host city competence. Instead, it points to deep structural features of the rotational model that generate predictable failures regardless of the host's political or economic context.These persistent failures are compounded by structural governance challenges. Organizing committees typically dissolve within months of the Games. In fact, 90% of staff depart within one month and 99% within four months. This elimination of institutional memory occurs precisely when long-term legacy planning becomes critical (9). This pattern extends beyond the Olympics to other megasporting events. For the 2027 Pan-American Games, Barranquilla, Colombia, was initially appointed as host but subsequently withdrew due to financial constraints. In the selection process that followed, Lima, Peru-which had recently hosted the 2019 Pan-American Games-successfully defeated Asunción, Paraguay, a city that had never hosted the event. This recent case demonstrates the implicit preference of selection committees for returning to proven hosts with existing infrastructure, driven by their capacity to deliver successful events at lower cost and risk compared to first-time hosts requiring extensive new construction. Peru's strategic advantage lay in its ability to reuse many venues from the 2019 Games, significantly reducing capital expenditure and environmental impact. This pragmatic turn toward venue reuse and proven hosts in the Pan-American context mirrors broader trends in Olympic hosting that we examine throughout this paper.The consistency of these failures across diverse contexts raises fundamental questions about causation. Zimbalist, Solberg, and Storm (7) pose the existential question that frames this paper: might the Olympic sustainability crisis stem from a structural "principal-agent problem" inherent to the rotational model itself? In this framework, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) functions as the principal, capturing the majority of Olympic revenues through broadcasting and sponsorship rights while transferring financial risks to host cities (the agents). This asymmetric incentive structure creates a fundamental misalignment: the IOC benefits from increasingly spectacular Games regardless of cost, while host cities bear the financial consequences of overspending with uncertain returns. The competitive bidding process exacerbates this dynamic, as cities that present conservative, realistic cost estimates are systematically outbid by competitors promising grander visions. This principal-agent misalignment, combined with the rotational model's requirement for cyclical construction in varying geopolitical contexts, may constitute the structural foundation of Olympic sustainability challenges-suggesting that incremental reforms addressing symptoms may prove insufficient without confronting the underlying architecture of the model itself.This conceptual paper explores the argument that the Olympic sustainability crisis requires transformative structural alternatives rather than incremental reforms. While questioning the rotational model may appear to be a radical departure from established Olympic tradition today, a historical retrospective reveals that geographic rotation was not always considered the only way to host the Games. In fact, it was fiercely debated at the movement's inception and has been repeatedly challenged during past eras of crisis. At the movement's birth in 1896, King George of Greece proposed permanent hosting in Athens. title: Towards Sustainable Neuromorphic Computing: A Thesis on Organoid Intelligence (OI) as a Paradigm for Low-Power Biocomputing
abstract: The relentless growth of computational demands, particularly from artificial intelligence (AI) and large-scale data centers, is pushing the limits of energy efficiency and sustainability with traditional silicon-based hardware. The von Neumann architecture, which separates memory and processing, creates a performance bottleneck known as the "memory wall," while the physical limits of transistor miniaturization (the end of Moore's Law) exacerbate these challenges. In response, the field of neuromorphic computing has emerged, seeking to emulate the brain's efficient, parallel, and low-power computational principles in hardware. This thesis explores a radical and nascent frontier within this field: Organoid Intelligence (OI), which utilizes three-dimensional cultures of human brain cells (brain organoids) as biological computational substrates. Reporting on the pioneering work of scientists in Switzerland and beyond, this paper investigates the potential of OI to create "living servers" that could replicate AI learning processes while using a fraction of the energy of current methods. We detail the foundational technology, including the derivation of neurons, the formation of organoids, and their interfacing with high-density microelectrode arrays (MEAs). The paper analyzes the unique computational properties of brain organoids, such as their inherent plasticity, low energy consumption, and ability to learn from stimuli, and contrasts them with both digital AI and analog neuromorphic chips. Furthermore, it addresses the significant technical and ethical hurdles, including the need for advanced bioengineering to scale organoids, the development of novel bio-compatible interfaces and algorithms, and the profound ethical considerations surrounding sentience and consciousness. We conclude that while OI is in its embryonic stages, it represents a transformative, long-term vision for biocomputing, offering a potentially revolutionary path toward sustainable and highly efficient cognitive computing. This thesis synthesizes current research to argue that strategic investment in OI is crucial for overcoming the impending computational energy crisis and unlocking new paradigms in machine intelligence. Keywords: Biocomputing, Organoid Intelligence (OI), Neuromorphic Computing, Brain Organoids, Microelectrode Arrays (MEAs), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Computing, Neuroethics. 1. Introduction 1.1. The Computational Energy Crisis and the Limits of Silicon The 21st century is defined by data. The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI), big data analytics, the Internet of Things (IoT), and complex scientific simulations has created an insatiable demand for computational power. Central to this digital revolution are massive data centers, the physical factories of the information age, which consume staggering amounts of electrical energy. Current estimates suggest that data centers account for approximately 1-2% of global electricity demand, a figure that is projected to rise sharply with the proliferation of energy-intensive deep learning models [1]. The environmental and economic costs of this consumption are becoming untenable, driving an urgent search for more efficient computing paradigms. This crisis is rooted in the fundamental architecture of modern computers. The von Neumann architecture, which has been the bedrock of computing for decades, features a central processing unit (CPU) separate from memory. This separation creates a bottleneck, known as the von Neumann bottleneck, where data must be constantly shuttled between these two units, consuming significant energy and limiting processing speed [2]. Furthermore, the decades-long trend of transistor miniaturization, encapsulated by Moore's Law, is reaching its physical and economic limits. As transistors approach the size of atoms, quantum effects and heat dissipation become critical problems, making further significant gains in efficiency through scaling increasingly difficult [3]. 1.2. Neuromorphic Computing: Learning from the Brain Inspired by the most efficient computational system known—the human brain—researchers have turned to neuromorphic engineering. The brain operates on a radically different principle than von Neumann machines. It is a massively parallel, asynchronous, and event-driven system where memory (synapses) and processing (neurons) are co-located. It consumes a mere ~20 watts of power, yet outperforms the world's most powerful supercomputers in tasks like pattern recognition, sensory processing, and adaptive learning [4]. Neuromorphic computing aims to mimic these neurobiological architectures using silicon and other materials, creating chips that are event-driven and highly parallelized [5], [6]. While promising, these hardware approaches are still synthetic approximations of a biological system. They face challenges in accurately replicating the brain's dynamic plasticity, its complex, non-linear dynamics, and its astounding energy efficiency. 1.3. Organoid Intelligence: A Radical Leap into Biocomputing This thesis focuses on a paradigm that moves beyond simulating the brain to utilizing biological neural networks directly for computation. This field, recently termed Organoid Intelligence (OI), proposes using three-dimensional (3D) cultures of human brain cells, known as brain organoids, as a novel biological hardware [7]. As reported by BBC Tech Now's Zoe Kleinman, scientists, particularly in Switzerland, are at the forefront of this research, developing techniques to grow these "mini-brains" and connect them to electrodes to harness their innate computational capabilities [8]. The central hypothesis of OI is that the inherent properties of living neural networks—their synaptic plasticity, low-power operation, and capacity for learning and self-organization—can be leveraged to perform specific computational tasks more efficiently than digital computers. The vision, as articulated by these researchers, is a future where data centers might house vats of these "living servers," performing complex cognitive tasks while using a minute fraction of the energy required by today's silicon-based servers. 1.4. Thesis Statement and Structure This thesis argues that Organoid Intelligence represents a viable, albeit long-term, pathway to overcome the energy and architectural limitations of conventional computing, offering a transformative framework for sustainable and cognitively advanced biocomputing. It posits that while significant technical and ethical challenges remain, the foundational research being conducted today lays the groundwork for a future where biological and synthetic systems are seamlessly integrated. The structure of this paper is as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed technical background on brain organoids and the field of neuromorphic computing. Section 3 delves into the core methodology of OI, from stem cell derivation to electrophysiological interfacing. Section 4 analyzes the proposed computational models and potential applications of brain organoids. Section 5 conducts a critical analysis, contrasting OI with existing technologies and outlining its advantages. Section 6 addresses the monumental technical challenges that must be overcome. Section 7 engages with the profound ethical, legal, and social implications (ELSI) of this technology. Section 8 concludes the paper and suggests directions for future research. 2. Technical Background 2.1. The Neurobiological Basis of Computation To appreciate the potential of OI, one must first understand the computational units of the brain. The fundamental processing element is the neuron. A neuron receives electrochemical signals from other neurons via its dendrites, integrates these signals in its cell body (soma), and, if a certain threshold is exceeded, fires an all-or-nothing electrical pulse called an action potential down its axon to communicate with downstream neurons [9]. Communication between neurons occurs at junctions called synapses. When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These chemicals bind to receptors on the post-synaptic neuron, influencing its likelihood of firing. The strength of this connection, known as synaptic plasticity, is not fixed. It can be strengthened (Long-Term Potentiation, LTP) or weakened (Long-Term Depression, LTD) based on neural activity [10]. This dynamic, experience-dependent modification of synaptic weights is the biological basis of learning and memory. The brain's computational power emerges from the complex, adaptive interactions within networks of billions of these neurons and trillions of synapses, operating in a massively parallel and distributed manner. 2.2. Brain Organoids: Miniature Models of the Brain Traditional neuroscience often relies on two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures or animal models. While invaluable, 2D cultures lack the complex 3D architecture and cell-cell interactions of a real brain, and animal models have inherent translational limitations for understanding human-specific brain functions and disorders. Brain organoids are 3D, self-organizing tissues derived from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), including both embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) [11]. Through carefully controlled biochemical cues, these stem cells are guided to differentiate into the various cell types of the nervous system (e.g., glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes) and self-assemble into structures that recapitulate key aspects of early human brain development [12]. These organoids can develop layered cortical structures, exhibit spontaneous electrical activity, and form functional synaptic networks. The process, as highlighted in the BBC report, involves growing these cells into clusters or "organoids" that are far more physiologically relevant than 2D cultures. They provide a unique, human-derived model for studying brain development, disease, and, as proposed by OI, computation. 2.3. Conventional and Neuromorphic Computing: A Primer Conventional Computing (Von Neumann): As previously mentioned, this architecture is characterized by sequential processing and the separation of memory (RAM, storage) and the central processing unit (CPU). Instructions and data are fetched from memory, decoded, and executed in the CPU, with results written back to memory. This sequential shuttling of data is energy-inefficient for tasks that are inherently parallel, such as pattern recognition. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML): Most modern AI, particularly deep learning, runs on von Neumann hardware. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are mathematical models inspired by the brain, with layers of artificial "neurons" (nodes) connected by weights (synapses). Training these networks requires massive datasets and immense computational power, often on clusters of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), which are themselves parallelized von Neumann architectures optimized for matrix operations [13]. Neuromorphic Computing (Silicon-based): This field designs hardware that physically mimics the brain's structure. Chips like Intel's Loihi [5] and IBM's TrueNorth [6] implement spiking neural networks (SNNs) directly in silicon. They use event-driven (asynchronous) communication, where "spikes" are sent only when necessary, and co-locate memory (via memristors or other technologies) with processing elements. This can lead to significant energy savings for specific tasks compared to running equivalent SNNs on GPUs. OI sits at the extreme end of the neuromorphic spectrum, proposing to use not a silicon imitation, but the biological original itself as the computational substrate. 3. The Methodology of Organoid Intelligence The realization of OI, as pioneered by the Swiss scientists and other groups worldwide, relies on a multi-step pipeline that integrates stem cell biology, bioengineering, and electrophysiology. 3.1. Derivation and Maturation of Brain Organoids The first step is the creation of the biological computational unit—the brain organoid. Stem Cell Sourcing: The process begins with human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) are often preferred for ethical reasons, as they can be generated from adult skin or blood cells [14]. These cells have the potential to differentiate into any cell type in the body. Directed Differentiation: Through a specific sequence of growth factors and small molecules, hPSCs are guided toward a neural fate. Protocols exist to generate organoids that model specific brain regions, such as the cerebral cortex, midbrain, or hippocampus [12], [15]. For general computation, cortical organoids are typically the focus. 3D Culture and Maturation: The differentiating cells are embedded in a 3D scaffold, such as Matrigel, which provides structural support and biochemical cues that encourage self-organization. The organoids are then maintained in spinning bioreactors or orbital shakers to enhance nutrient and oxygen diffusion, allowing them to grow to sizes of a few millimeters over periods of months [16]. During this time, they undergo complex developmental processes, including neurogenesis, migration, and synaptogenesis, leading to the emergence of spontaneous, synchronized network-wide activity, akin to the electroencephalogram (EEG) signals seen in a developing brain [17]. 3.2. title: A Great Conversation With Deborah Friedman
abstract: Kathleen Digre (KD): Today we have the great pleasure of talking with Dr. Deborah Friedman, who is a former Professor of Neurology and Ophthalmology at UT (University of Texas) Southwestern in Dallas and also a former President of the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society (NANOS). We're really glad to have you with us today, Dr. Friedman. Deb Friedman (DF): Dr. Digre, the pleasure is mine. [chuckle] Although I know you have to be somewhat seasoned in order to be having a great conversation. KD: That's okay, I've already done one, Deborah, so you're not alone. Meagan Seay (MS): Please start off by telling us about your background prior to medical school. DF: How far back do you want me to go? Birth? [laughter]. KD: Well, tell us where you were born and brought up, because you've got an interesting background and you should display it. DF: All right. I was born and raised in Miami, Florida, the oldest of 3 children and the only girl. I went to a public high school, in southwest Miami, called Southwest High School. Then I went to college at Georgia Tech, and I was an engineering major there. I had to, as they say in the South, cram 4 years of college into 5 because about halfway through engineering school I decided that I wanted to go to medical school. So, that was in addition to taking the classes that I needed to take for my degree, called Engineering Science and Mechanics, which is now a defunct major. I also took a lot of bioengineering courses because at the time they didn't really have a bioengineering major. So, I was either going to go to graduate school for biomedical engineering or try to get into medical school. After taking all those extra classes to go into medical school, I was fortunate enough to get in at Tulane. So, that was where I went to medical school, hence my Louisiana connection (Fig. 1).FIG. 1.: Still smiling!MS: Can you tell us more about medical school and specifically how you picked the specialty you did? DF: When I went to medical school, I actually had no preconceived notions of what I wanted to do. There were no other doctors in my family. I actually thought that I was going to be a surgeon because I kind of have that mentality, and I also like doing procedures. I didn't even know what neurology was. In our first year, we had a neuroanatomy class. Prior to my year, all of the medical students loved neuroanatomy. It was their favorite class. And the reason it was their favorite class was that it was taught by a neurologist. His name was Jeffrey Ellison, and he was a neurologist at Ochsner who would come in and teach neuroanatomy. Well, unfortunately, the summer before I matriculated in medical school—don't ever do this yourself—he was working on his roof and he fell off his roof and he died. So, they called in the understudy, who I will not name, but they called in a graduate student to teach the course kind of at the last minute. DF: He was just really dry and really monotone, and it was super boring. It didn't really appeal to me at all. I didn't understand why all these people liked neuroanatomy so much. But the highlight of the course was when Dr. Leon Weisberg, who was the head of the Department of Neurology and Psychiatry at the time, came in and he taught us clinical correlations. So, he presented these cases as unknowns (kind of like the Walsh meeting). One of them was actually Franklin Roosevelt, and it was a case of polio. We were supposed to read the cases and figure out the anatomic localization. I think there were 3 cases, and I pretty much got them all wrong, but it didn't matter because it was so much fun. And so that was when I started to become interested in neurology. But nonetheless, when I went through all of the clinical rotations, I really liked everything. The thing that I liked the most was when I was on service with Dr. Weisberg, which I requested just to make sure that I would have a really great mentor. That sealed the deal for becoming a neurologist (Fig. 2).FIG. 2.: With dad (Robert) at medical school graduation from Tulane.DF: At the end of my third year, I was applying to residencies and I did an elective away back in Atlanta because, truth be told, I really just wanted to see my friends from Georgia Tech. I contacted my former boss, who was the head of bioengineering at one of the hospitals in Atlanta, to see if he could find me an elective to do there (Things were different back then. Doing an elective away was much looser). So, he arranged for me to do an elective at Emory with their pediatric ophthalmologist. And, you know, although I do headache medicine now, I'm not a headache person. I don't get headaches. But during that elective, I had a headache every single day leaving the office because I just watched him refracting screaming children all day long. Pediatric ophthalmology was interesting, but clearly, it wasn't for me. But while I was there, I spent a few days with their neuro-ophthalmologist, Robert Spector, who was at Emory before Nancy Newman and her group came to Emory. We saw super cool patients, great cases. And I just thought this was the coolest best thing I had ever seen. I knew right then and there that I wanted to be a neuro-ophthalmologist. So, I was actually filling out my applications for neurology residency at the time after hours in the Emory Eye Clinic and wrote my essay about how I wanted to be a neuro-ophthalmologist. DF: Around that time (I hate to date myself but, you know, we are having a Great Conversation), actually shortly before that time, CT (computerized tomography) scanning was developed. People were saying they're not going to need neurologists anymore, and they're definitely not going to need neuro-ophthalmologists because now we have imaging of the brain.
